messages.subject_clean: Using a phenotype as a covariate
messages.body_plain:
I got the following question via email, and I thought that it and my (brief) response might be of interest.

> I would like to use flowering day as covariate in a RIL population but I can't find code examples to do this. I checked online but I found it a bit confusing.
> Could you help me please?.

Try something like this:

 out <- scanone(mycross, method="hk", addcovar=mycross$pheno[,"floweringDay"])

karl

messages.subject: Using R/qtl on data with more than 2 alleles per locus
messages.subject_clean: Using R/qtl on data with more than 2 alleles per locus
messages.body_plain:
I got the following email, and I though it and my response might be of interest.

> After perusing "A brief Tour of R/qtl" and trying out the examples within, we are highly impressed by R/qtl's functionality.
> In particular, it is much faster than the softwares we are currently using (JoinMap & MapQTL from Kyazama), and also much more versatile.
> Hence, we wish to apply R/qtl to our future projects.
> However, one obstacle we have encountered is that R/qtl seems to assume that there are only 2 alleles (hence 3 genotypes i.e. AA, Aa, aa) per locus, but this is not true for our data.
> The markers we use include SSRs and SNPs. Most SSRs, and even some SNPs, have more than 2 alleles per locus.
> Also, while it is possible to specially breed a mapping population with only 2 alleles per locus, this is highly impractical for some species, especially those with a long life cycle.
> Is there a way to use R/qtl on data with more than 2 alleles per locus?
> Any advice or help you can provide will be highly appreciated!

R/qtl focuses on simple crosses between inbred lines.

If you have a large sibship derived from two outbred individuals, it's *possible* to analyze it in R/qtl using the cross type "4way", for a phase-known 4-way cross (the 4 being the grandparents), but you first have to infer phase in the parents, which is usually hard, and there's little documentation.

There still aren't many options for QTL mapping in outbred crosses, unfortunately.

Alternatively, you could do association mapping (for example, perform analysis of variance at each SNP) using something like PLINK.

karl

mapthis <- subset(mapthis, ind = -wh[,2])

I should also add: that code with the "tozero" business is taken from page 7 of the Genetic Map Construction tutorial <http://www.rqtl.org/tutorials/geneticmaps.pdf>. And at that point the mapthis object had just one chromosome (because we hadn't yet inferred the linkage groups) and also the g object was the matrix of genotypes, for that one and only chromosome.

I you wanted to do that sort of thing (for each pair of duplicates, remove any marker genotypes where they are discordant) in the case that there is more than one chromosome, you'd need an additional look over chromosomes:

for(j in chrnames(mapthis)) {
    g <- pull.geno(mapthis, chr=j)

    for(i in 1:nrow(wh)) {
        tozero <- !is.na <http://is.na>(g[wh[i,1],]) & !is.na <http://is.na>(g[wh[i,2],]) & g[wh[i,1],] != g[wh[i,2],]

        mapthis$geno[[j]]$data[wh[i,1], tozero] <- NA
    }
}

karl

messages.body_plain:
Hi Karl,

When I use the command eat.rf to estimate the recombination fraction of my map, I got this error massage:

Error in rep(0, n.mar * n.mar) : invalid 'times' argument
In addition: Warning message:
In n.mar * n.mar : NAs produced by integer overflow

I searched a little bit about the reason, and some said it's about the NA problem, as stated in the error message. But I don't know how to tackle it. Could you help me?

Thank you very much!

Ziming

messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] Err in est.rf
messages.body_plain:
I think it's likely that you have more markers than can be handled.
est.rf will calculate a matrix that is M x M where M is the number of markers.
For more than about 1000 markers, it's not really a workable effort.
For more than about 10,000 markers, we can't even create the matrix.

karl

messages.body_plain:
Unfortunately, R/qtl doesn't have much facility for crosses with outbred individuals.

You won't be able to treat the genotypes as AA/AB.

Rather, you'll need to infer phase in the A1 and Z1/1 parents. It'd be ideal to have genotyped the grandparents, too.
At a RAPD, say B is the band allele and N is the non-band allele. Then you need to determine which markers are

  BN x NN   vs   NB x NN   vs   NN x BN   vs   NN x NB

This goes hand-in-hand with constructing the genetic map, because you have to find the linked markers in order to determine phase.

Once phase has been determined, then you can use R/qtl for QTL analysis or to estimate inter-marker distances, but you need to treat it as a phase-known 4-way cross. And the encoding of genotypes is complicated. Described in the help file for read.cross:

For a 4-way cross, the mother and father are assumed to have genotypes AB and CD, respectively. The genotype data for the progeny is assumed to be phase-known, with the following coding scheme: NA = missing, 1 = AC, 2 = BC, 3 = AD, 4 = BD, 5 = A = AC or AD, 6 = B = BC or BD, 7 = C = AC or BC, 8 = D = AD or BD, 9 = AC or BD, 10 = AD or BC, 11 = not AC, 12 = not BC, 13 = not AD, 14 = not BD.

karl

Unfortunately, the 'model' argument to sim.cross is ignored for the "riself" cross type. It's only used for backcross, intercross, 4-way cross, and BCsFt.

sim.cross with type="riself" simulates genotypes, but just returns a single phenotype with integers 1, 2, ..., n.ind.
